extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (especially those crafting ensemble casts)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating and evaluating ensemble casts in fiction, focusing on who is the lead (the 'pro-protagonist'), how other characters must carry weight, how/when to use multiple POVs, and how to justify every character's presence in the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensemble definition: everyone has their own weight
rubrics_metrics.description: The thing that makes it an ensemble to me is everyone sort of has their own weight. The story couldn’t function the same without every single one of these characters. Sometimes it’s emotional weight, sometimes it’s a physical presence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An ensemble means 'every single person almost matters' and 'they play a part.' Use examples like Buffy or Friends to think about characters who contribute essential emotional or physical roles. If removing a character leaves the story fundamentally different or broken, they likely belong in an ensemble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple POV as a hallmark of ensemble (but not always)
rubrics_metrics.description: One hallmark is multiple POVs used not to change locations, but because other characters can move the story forward. Anytime I see that, I expect, oh, this is an ensemble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Switch POV when a different character's perception is what is moving the story forward, not merely because they are in a different place. Anti-pattern: introducing many POVs only because characters are geographically separate (example: Powder Mage books introduce three POVs in different locations but it doesn't read like an ensemble).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pro-protagonist (leader) vs co-protagonists
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with the protagonist protagonist. I call my hero that, or my heroine that. Because sometimes, even though you have a group of people, there is still a leader. To me, they shape the relationship between themselves and everybody else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the 'pro-protag' who has the strongest through-thread; others are co-protagonists whose arcs and moments are threaded through that leader's journey (examples: Tony Stark as the lead in Avengers; Picard in TNG). Use the pro-protag to shape ensemble relationships and emotional focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify the ensemble: why does the story need these extra people?
rubrics_metrics.description: Answering this question is what separates an ensemble from the story of a single person and the people who assist them. Are the other people just spear carriers or are they real characters?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each character ask why they must exist in the story. Avoid nameless or faceless 'spear carriers'—if a character doesn't justify their presence, they shouldn't take up narrative space. Especially in visual media you must justify extra people or they become wasted camera angles; in prose you still must justify their existence through role, weight, or distinct contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters must be people with dynamics and touchpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: Everyone matters, and they play a part. There’s really interesting dynamics. They bounce off of each other. They have touch points in the protagonist protagonist's journey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make characters interact and influence each other—group dynamics should change as each member is added. Use touchpoints where ensemble members connect to the pro-protag (examples: Hey Arnold! where many characters have touchpoints with Arnold; Sailor Moon where the group changes as she finds each member). These interactions create emotional stakes and richness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start characterization with the pro-protag (practical exercise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with the protagonist protagonist; that is the beginning of characterization when I start writing a book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical homework: free-write a scene where your pro-protag is 'applying for the job' of being the protagonist—have them argue why they're good and why they'd fail. This clarifies strengths, weaknesses, and helps position other characters relative to that anchor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual (prose) ensembles require different handling than visual ensembles
rubrics_metrics.description: When it comes to books, it’s almost harder to navigate those waters, because the text has to do so much work than the visual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In prose you cannot rely on visual shorthand; you must show each character's distinctness through voice, actions, relationships, and POV choices. Plan how narrative voice, scene selection, and POV shifts will communicate a group's dynamics without cinematic cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make ensemble members move the story forward
rubrics_metrics.description: Switching POV because this other character needs… the way they are perceiving what the group is doing is what is moving the story forward right now.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use characters' perspectives deliberately: a character's POV should be chosen when their perception or choices materially affect the group's trajectory. Don't include POVs or scenes that exist only to show setting or filler; each should advance plot or deepen characterization.
